**Strepsiades**
Why then, since you imitate the cocks in all things, do you not both eat dung and sleep on a perch?
1.1432:
**Phidippides**
It is not the same thing, my friend; nor would it appear so to Socrates.

**Strepsiades**
Therefore do not beat me; otherwise you will one day blame yourself.

**Phidippides**

**Phidippides**

**Strepsiades**

**Phidippides**

**Phidippides**

**Strepsiades**

**Phidippides**

**Phidippides**
But what if, having the worst Cause,

**Phidippides**
I shall conquer you in arguing, proving that it is right to beat one’s mother?

**Strepsiades**

**Strepsiades**

**Strepsiades**

**Phidippides**
I will not injure my teachers.

**Phidippides**

**Strepsiades**
There is.

**Strepsiades**

**Phidippides**

of the prating fellows. Come hither, come hither, Xanthias! Come forth with a ladder and with a mattock and then mount upon the thinking-shop and dig down the roof, if you love your master, until you tumble the house upon them.

1.0: *SCENE: A wild and desolate region; only thickets, rocks, and a single tree are seen. Euelpides and Pisthetaerus enter, each with a bird in his hand.*
1.1:
**Euelpides**
*To his jay.*
Do you think I should walk straight for yon tree?
1.2:
**Pisthetaerus**
*To his crow.*
Cursed beast, what are you croaking to me?... to retrace my steps?
1.3:
**Euelpides**
Why, you wretch, we are wandering at random, we are exerting ourselves only to return to the same spot; we're wasting our time.
1.5:
**Pisthetaerus**
To think that I should trust to this crow, which has made me cover more than a thousand furlongs!
1.7:
**Euelpides**
And that I, in obedience to this jay, should have worn my toes down to the nails!
1.9:
**Pisthetaerus**
If only I knew where we were...
1.10:
**Euelpides**
Could you find your country again from here?
1.11:
**Pisthetaerus**
No, I feel quite sure I could not, any more than could Execestides find his.
1.12:
**Euelpides**
Alas!
**Pisthetaerus**
Aye, aye, my friend, it's surely the road of alases we are following.
1.13:
**Euelpides**
That Philocrates, the bird-seller, played us a scurvy trick,
1.15:
when he pretended these two guides could help us to find Tereus, the Epops, who is a bird, without being born of one. He has indeed sold us this jay, a true son of Tharrhelides, for an obolus, and this crow for three, but what can they do? Why, nothing whatever but bite and scratch!
*To his jay.*
1.20: What's the matter with you then, that you keep opening your beak? Do you want us to fling ourselves headlong down these rocks? There is no road that way.
1.22:
**Pisthetaerus**
Not even the vestige of a trail in any direction
1.23:
**Euelpides**
And what does the crow say about the road to follow?
1.24:
**Pisthetaerus**
By Zeus, it no longer croaks the same thing it did.
1.25:
**Euelpides**

**Pisthetaerus**

1.27:
**Euelpides**

1.35: we have fled from our country as hard as ever we could go. It's not that we hate it; we recognize it to be great and rich, likewise that everyone has the right to ruin himself paying taxes; but the crickets only chirrup among the fig-trees for a month or two,
1.40: whereas the Athenians spend their whole lives in chanting forth judgments from their law-courts. That is why we started off with a basket, a stew-pot and some myrtle boughs and have come to seek a quiet country
1.45: in which to settle. We are going to Tereus, the Epops, to learn from him, whether, in his aerial flights, he has noticed some town of this kind.
1.49:
**Pisthetaerus**
Here! look!

**Pisthetaerus**
Why, the crow has been directing me
1.50:
to something up there for some time now.

*From within.*

**Euelpides**

**Euelpides**

We wish to pay you a visit.
1.114:
**Epops**
What for?
**Euelpides**
Because you formerly were a man, like we are,
1.115: formerly you had debts, as we have, formerly you did not want to pay them, like ourselves; furthermore, being turned into a bird, you have when flying seen all lands and seas. Thus you have all human knowledge as well as that of birds.
1.120: And hence we have come to you to beg you to direct us to some cosy town, in which one can repose as if on thick coverlets.
1.123:
**Epops**
And are you looking for a greater city than Athens?
1.124:
**Euelpides**
No, not a greater, but one more pleasant to live in.
1.125:
**Epops**
Then you are looking for an aristocratic country.
**Euelpides**
I? Not at all! I hold the son of Scellias in horror.
1.127:
**Epops**
But, after all, what sort of city would please you best?
1.128:
**Euelpides**
A place where the following would be the most important business transacted. —Some friend would come knocking at the door quite early in the morning
1.130: saying, By Olympian Zeus, be at my house early, as soon as you have bathed, and bring your children too. I am giving a nuptial feast, so don't fail, or else don't cross my threshold when I am in distress.
1.135:
**Epops**
Ah! that's what may be called being fond of hardships!
*To Pisthetaerus.*
And what say you?
1.136:
**Pisthetaerus**
My tastes are similar.
**Epops**
And they are?
1.137:
**Pisthetaerus**
I want a town where the father of a handsome lad will stop in the street and say to me reproachfully as if I had failed him, Ah! Is this well done, Stilbonides?
1.140: You met my son coming from the bath after the gymnasium and you neither spoke to him, nor kissed him, nor took him with you, nor ever once felt his balls. Would anyone call you an old friend of mine?
1.143:
**Epops**
Ah! wag, I see you are fond of suffering. But there is a city of delights such as you want.
1.145:
It's on the Red Sea.
**Euelpides**
Oh, no. Not a sea-port, where some fine morning the Salaminian galley can appear, bringing a process-server along. Have you no Greek town you can propose to us?
1.149:
**Epops**
Why not choose Lepreum in Elis for your settlement?
1.150:
**Euelpides**
By Zeus! I could not look at Lepreum without disgust, because of Melanthius.
1.152:
**Epops**
Then, again, there is the Opuntian Locris, where you could live.
1.153:
**Euelpides**
I would not be Opuntian for a talent.
1.155: But come, what is it like to live with the birds? You should know pretty well.
1.156:
**Epops**
Why, it's not a disagreeable life. In the first place, one has no purse.
1.158:
**Euelpides**
That does away with a lot of roguery.
1.159:
**Epops**
For food the gardens yield us white sesame,
1.161:
**Euelpides**
Why, 'tis the life of the newly-wed indeed.
**Pisthetaerus**
Ha! I am beginning to see a great plan, which will transfer the supreme power to the birds, if you will but take my advice.
1.164:
**Epops**
Take your advice? In what way?
**Pisthetaerus**
In what way? Well, firstly,
1.165: do not fly in all directions with open beak; it is not dignified. Among us, when we see a thoughtless man, we ask, What sort of bird is this? and Teleas answers, It's a man who has no brain, a bird that has lost his head, a creature
1.170: you cannot catch, for it never remains in any one place.
1.171:
**Epops**
By Zeus himself! your jest hits the mark. What then is to be done?
1.173:
**Epops**
We birds? But what sort of city should we build?
1.174:
**Pisthetaerus**
Oh, really, really! you talk like such a fool!
1.175:
Look down.
**Epops**
I am looking.
**Pisthetaerus**
Now look up.
1.176:
**Epops**
I am looking.
**Pisthetaerus**
Turn your head round.
**Epops**
Ah! it will be pleasant for me if I end in twisting my neck off!
1.178:
**Pisthetaerus**
What have you seen?
**Epops**
The clouds and the sky.
1.179:
**Pisthetaerus**
Very well! is not this the pole of the birds then?
1.180:
**Epops**
How their pole?
**Pisthetaerus**
Or, if you like it, their place. And since it turns and passes through the whole universe, it is called ‘pole.’ If you build and fortify it, you will turn your pole into a city.
1.185: In this way you will reign over mankind as you do over the grasshoppers and you will cause the gods to die of rabid hunger.
1.187:
**Epops**
How so?
**Pisthetaerus**
The air is between earth and heaven. When we want to go to Delphi, we ask the Boeotians for leave of passage;
1.190: in the same way, when men sacrifice to the gods, unless the latter pay you tribute, you exercise the right of every nation towards strangers and don't allow the smoke of the sacrifices to pass through your city and territory.
1.194:
**Epops**
By earth! by snares! by network! by cages!
1.195: I never heard of anything more cleverly conceived; and, if the other birds approve, I am going to build the city along with you.
1.198:
**Pisthetaerus**
Who will explain the matter to them?
**Epops**
You must yourself. Before I came they were quite ignorant,
1.200: but since I have lived with them I have taught them to speak.
1.201:
**Pisthetaerus**
But how can they be gathered together?
**Epops**
Easily. I will hasten down to the thicket to waken my dear Procne
1.205: and as soon as they hear our voices, they will come to us hot wing.
1.206:
**Pisthetaerus**
My dear bird, lose no time, please! Fly at once into the thicket and awaken Procne.
*Epops rushes into the thicket.*
1.209:
**Epops**
*From within; singing.*
Chase off drowsy sleep, dear companion.
1.210: Let the sacred hymn gush from thy divine throat in melodious strains; roll forth in soft cadence your refreshing melodies to bewail the fate of Itys, which has been the cause of so many tears to us both.
1.215: Your pure notes rise through the thick leaves of the yew-tree right up to the throne of Zeus, where Phoebus listens to you, Phoebus with his golden hair. And his ivory lyre responds to your plaintive accents;
1.220:
he gathers the choir of the gods and from their immortal lips pours forth a sacred chant of blessed voices.
*The flute is played behind the scene, imitating the song of the nightingale.*
1.223:
**Pisthetaerus**
Oh! by Zeus! what a throat that little bird possesses. He has filled the whole thicket with honey-sweet melody!
1.225:
**Euelpides**
Hush!
**Pisthetaerus**
What's the matter?
**Euelpides**
Be still!
**Pisthetaerus**
What for?
1.226:
**Euelpides**
Epops is going to sing again.
1.230: all you who pillage the fertile lands of the husbandmen, the numberless tribes who gather and devour the barley seeds, the swift flying race that sings so sweetly. And you whose gentle twitter
1.235: resounds through the fields with the little cry of tiotiotiotiotiotiotiotio; and you who hop about the branches of the ivy in the gardens;
1.240: the mountain birds, who feed on the wild olive-berries or the arbutus, hurry to come at my call, trioto, trioto, totobrix; you also, who snap up the sharp-stinging
1.245: gnats in the marshy vales, and you who dwell in the fine plain of Marathon, all damp with dew, and you, the francolin with speckled wings;
1.250: you too, the halcyons, who flit over the swelling waves of the sea, come hither to hear the tidings; let all the tribes of long-necked birds assemble here;
1.255: know that a clever old man has come to us, bringing an entirely new idea and proposing great reforms. Let all come to the debate here, here, here, here.
1.263:
**Pisthetaerus**
Can you see any bird?
**Euelpides**
By Phoebus, no! and yet I am straining my eyesight to scan the sky.
1.265:
**Pisthetaerus**
It was hardly worth Epops' while to go and bury himself in the thicket like a hatching plover.
1.269:
**Euelpides**
By Zeus, it is a bird, but what kind? Isn't it a peacock?
1.270:
**Pisthetaerus**
*As Epops comes out of the thicket.*
Epops will tell us. What is this bird?
1.271:
**Epops**
It's not one of those you are used to seeing; it's a bird from the marshes.
1.272:
**Euelpides**
Oh! oh! but he is very handsome with his wings as crimson as flame.
1.273:
**Epops**
Undoubtedly; indeed he is called flamingo.
1.274:
**Euelpides**
*Excitedly.*
Hi! I say! You!
**Pisthetaerus**
What are you shouting for?
**Euelpides**
Why, here's another bird.
1.275:
**Pisthetaerus**
Aye, indeed; this one's a foreign bird too.
*To Epops.*
What is this bird from beyond the mountains with a look as solemn as it is stupid?
1.277:
**Epops**
He is called the Mede.
**Euelpides**
The Mede! But, by Heracles, how, if a Mede, has he flown here without a camel?
1.279:
**Pisthetaerus**
Here's another bird with a crest.
*From here on, the numerous birds that make up the Chorus keep rushing in.*
1.280:
**Euelpides**
Ah! that's curious. I say, Epops, you are not the only one of your kind then?
1.281:
**Epops**
This bird is the son of Philocles, who is the son of Epops; so that, you see, I am his grandfather; just as one might say, Hipponicus, the son of Callias, who is the son of Hipponicus.
1.284:
**Euelpides**
Then this bird is Callias! Why, what a lot of his feathers he has lost!
1.285:
**Epops**
That's because he is honest; so the informers set upon him and the women too pluck out his feathers.
1.287:
**Euelpides**
By Poseidon, do you see that many-coloured bird? What is his name?
1.289:
**Euelpides**
Is there another glutton besides Cleonymus?
1.290: But why, if he is Cleonymus, has he not thrown away his crest?
1.291: But what is the meaning of all these crests? Have these birds come to contend for the double stadium prize?
1.292:
**Epops**
They are like the Carians, who cling to the crests of their mountains for greater safety.
1.294:
**Pisthetaerus**
Oh, Poseidon! look what awful swarms of birds are gathering here!
1.295:
**Euelpides**
By Phoebus! what a cloud! The entrance to the stage is no longer visible so closely do they fly together.
1.297:
**Pisthetaerus**
Here is the partridge.
**Euelpides**
Why, there is the francolin.
1.298:
**Pisthetaerus**
There is the poachard.
**Euelpides**
Here is the kingfisher.
1.299:
*To Epops.*
What's that bird behind the kingfisher?
**Epops**
That's the barber.
1.300:
**Euelpides**
What? a bird a barber?
**Pisthetaerus**
Why, Sporgilus is one.
1.301:
**Epops**
Here comes the owl.
**Euelpides**
And who is it brings an owl to Athens?
1.302:
**Epops**
*Pointing to the various species.*
Here is the magpie, the turtle-dove, the swallow, the horned-owl, the buzzard, the pigeon, the falcon, the ring-dove, the cuckoo, the red-foot, the red-cap, the purple-cap, the kestrel, the diver, the ousel, the osprey, the woodpecker...
1.305:
**Pisthetaerus**
Oh! what a lot of birds! Oh! what a lot of blackbirds! How they scold, how they come rushing up! What a noise! what a noise! Can they be bearing us ill-will? Oh! there! there! they are opening their beaks and staring at us.
1.310:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Popopopopopo. Where is he who called me? Where am I to find him?
1.312:
**Epops**
I have been waiting for you a long while! I never fail in my word to my friends.
1.313:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Tititititititi. What good news
1.316:
**Epops**
Something that concerns our common safety, and that is just as pleasant as it is to the point. Two men, who are subtle reasoners, have come here to seek me.
1.318:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Where? How? What are you saying?
1.320:
**Epops**
I say, two old men have come from the abode of humans to propose a vast and splendid scheme to us.
1.322:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Oh! it's a horrible, unheard-of crime! What are you saying?
1.323:
**Epops**
Never let my words scare you.
**Leader of the Chorus**
What have you done to me?
1.324:
**Epops**
I have welcomed two men, who wish to live with us.
1.325:
**Leader of the Chorus**
And you have dared to do that!
**Epops**
Yes, and I am delighted at having done so.
1.326:
**Leader of the Chorus**
And are they already with us?
**Epops**
Just as much as I am.
1.327:
**Chorus**
*Singing.*
Ah! ah! we are betrayed; 'tis sacrilege! Our friend,
1.330: he who picked up corn-seeds in the same plains as ourselves, has violated our ancient laws; he has broken the oaths that bind all birds; he has laid a snare for me, he has handed us over to the attacks of that impious race which, throughout all time,
1.335: has never ceased to war against us.
1.336:
**Leader of the Chorus**
As for this traitorous bird, we will decide his case later, but the two old men shall be punished forthwith; we are going to tear them to pieces.
1.339:
**Euelpides**
You are the sole cause of all our trouble.
1.340:
Why did you bring me from down yonder?
**Pisthetaerus**
To have you with me.
1.341:
**Euelpides**
Say rather to have me melt into tears.
**Pisthetaerus**
Go on! you are talking nonsense. How will you weep with your eyes pecked out?
1.343:
**Chorus**
*Singing.*
Io! io! forward to the attack, throw yourselves upon the foe,
1.345: spill his blood; take to your wings and surround them on all sides. Woe to them! let us get to work with our beaks, let us devour them.
1.350: Nothing can save them from our wrath, neither the mountain forests, nor the clouds that float in the sky, nor the foaming deep.
1.352:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Come, peck, tear to ribbons. Where is the chief of the cohort? Let him engage the right wing.
*They rush at the two Athenians.*
1.354:
**Euelpides**
This is the fatal moment. Where shall I fly to, unfortunate wretch that I am?
**Pisthetaerus**
Wait! Stay here!
1.355:
**Euelpides**
That they may tear me to pieces?
**Pisthetaerus**
And how do you think to escape them?
1.356:
**Euelpides**
I don't know at all.
**Pisthetaerus**
Come, I will tell you. We must stop and fight them. Let us arm ourselves with these stew-pots.
1.358:
**Euelpides**
Why with the stew-pots?
**Pisthetaerus**
The owl will not attack us then.
1.359:
**Euelpides**
But do you see all those hooked claws?
**Pisthetaerus**
Take the spit
1.360:
and pierce the foe on your side.
**Euelpides**
And how about my eyes?
1.361:
**Pisthetaerus**
Protect them with this dish or this vinegar-pot.
1.362:
**Euelpides**
Oh! what cleverness! what inventive genius! You are a great general, even greater than Nicias, where stratagem is concerned.
1.364:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Forward, forward, charge with your beaks! Come, no delay.
1.365: Tear, pluck, strike, flay them, and first of all smash the stew-pot.
1.366:
**Epops**
*Stepping in front of the Chorus.*
Oh, most cruel of all animals, why tear these two men to pieces, why kill them? What have they done to you? They belong to the same tribe, to the same family as my wife.
1.369:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Are wolves to be spared? Are they not our most mortal foes?
1.371:
**Epops**
If they are your foes by nature, they are your friends in heart, and they come here to give you useful advice.
1.373:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Advice or a useful word from their lips, from them, the enemies of my forebears?
1.375:
**Epops**
The wise can often profit by the lessons of a foe, for caution is the mother of safety. It is just such a thing as one will not learn from a friend and which an enemy compels you to know. To begin with, it's the foe and not the friend that taught cities to build high walls, to equip long vessels of war;
1.380: and it's this knowledge that protects our children, our slaves and our wealth.
1.381:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Well then, I agree, let us first hear them, for that is best; one can even learn something in an enemy's school.
1.383:
**Pisthetaerus**
*To Euelpides.*
Their wrath seems to cool. Draw back a little.
1.384:
**Epops**
It's only justice, and you will thank me later.
1.385:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Never have we opposed your advice up to now.
1.386:
**Pisthetaerus**
They are in a more peaceful mood; put down your stew-pot and your two dishes; spit in hand, doing duty for a spear, let us mount guard inside the camp
1.390: close to the pot and watch in our arsenal closely; for we must not fly.
1.393:
**Euelpides**
You are right. But where shall we be buried, if we die?
1.395:
**Pisthetaerus**
In the Ceramicus; for, to get a public funeral, we shall tell the Strategi that we fell at Orneae, fighting the country's foes.
1.400:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Return to your ranks and lay down your courage beside your wrath as the hoplites do. Then let us ask these men who they are, whence they come,
1.405: and with what intent. Here, Epops, answer me.
1.407:
**Epops**
Are you calling me? What do you want of me?
1.408:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Who are they? From what country?
1.409:
**Epops**
Strangers, who have come from Greece, the land of the wise.
1.410:
**Leader of the Chorus**
And what fate has led them hither to the land of the birds?
1.412:
**Epops**
Their love for you and their wish to share your kind of life; to dwell and
1.416:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Indeed, and what are their plans?
1.417:
**Epops**
They are wonderful, incredible, unheard of.
1.418:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Why, do they think to see some advantage that determines them to settle here? Are they hoping with our help
1.420: to triumph over their foes or to be useful to their friends?
1.422:
**Epops**
They speak of benefits so great it is impossible either to describe or conceive them; all shall be yours,
1.425: all that we see here, there, above and below us; this they vouch for.
1.427:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Are they mad?
1.428:
**Epops**
They are the sanest people in the world.
1.430:
**Epops**
The slyest of foxes, cleverness its very self, men of the world, cunning, the cream of knowing folk.
1.432:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Tell them to speak and speak quickly; why, as I listen to you, I am beside myself with delight.
1.435:
**Epops**
*To two attendants.*
Here, you there, take all these weapons and hang them up inside close to the fire, near the figure of the god who presides there and under his protection;
*To Pisthetaerus.*
as for you, address the birds, tell them why I have gathered them together.
1.440: unless they agree with me as the little ape of an armorer agreed with his wife, not to bite me, nor pull me by the balls, nor shove things into my...
1.442:
**Euelpides**
*Bending over and pointing his finger at his anus.*
Do you mean this?
1.444:
**Leader of the Chorus**
Agreed.
**Pisthetaerus**
Swear it.
1.445:
**Leader of the Chorus**
I swear it and, if I keep my promise, let judges and spectators give me the victory unanimously.
1.447:
**Leader of the Chorus**
And if I break my word, may I succeed by one vote only.
1.450: do not fail to read the decrees of dismissal we have posted.
1.451:
**Chorus**
*Singing.*
Man is a truly cunning creature, but nevertheless explain. Perhaps you are going to show me some good way
1.455: to extend my power, some way that I have not had the wit to find out and which you have discovered. Speak! 'tis to your own interest as well as to mine, for if you secure me some advantage, I will surely share it with you.
1.460:
**Leader of the Chorus**
But what object can have induced you to come among us? Speak boldly, for I shall not break the truce, —until you have told us all.
1.462:
**Pisthetaerus**
I am bursting with desire to speak; I have already mixed the dough of my address and nothing prevents me from kneading it.... Slave! bring the chaplet and water, which you must pour over my hands. Be quick!
1.464:
**Euelpides**
Is it a question of feasting? What does it all mean?
1.465:
**Pisthetaerus**
By Zeus, no! but I am hunting for fine, tasty words to break down the hardness of their hearts.
*To the Chorus.*
I grieve so much for you, who at one time were kings...
1.467:
**Leader of the Chorus**
We kings? Over whom?
**Pisthetaerus**
... of all that exists, firstly of me and of this man, even of Zeus himself. Your race is older than Saturn, the Titans and the Earth.
1.470:
**Leader of the Chorus**
What, older than the Earth!
**Pisthetaerus**
By Phoebus, yes.
**Leader of the Chorus**
By Zeus, but I never knew that before!
1.471:
**Pisthetaerus**
That's because you are ignorant and heedless, and have never read your Aesop. He is the one who tells us that the lark was born before all other creatures, indeed before the Earth; his father died of sickness, but the Earth did not exist then; he remained unburied for five days, when the bird in its dilemma decided,
1.475: for want of a better place, to entomb its father in its own head.
1.476:
**Euelpides**
So that the lark's father is buried at Cephalae.
1.477:
**Pisthetaerus**
Hence, if they existed before the Earth, before the gods, the kingship belongs to them by right of priority.
1.479:
**Euelpides**
Undoubtedly, but sharpen your beak well;
1.480: Zeus won't be in a hurry to hand over his scepter to the woodpecker.
1.481:
**Pisthetaerus**
It was not the gods, but the birds, who were formerly the masters and kings over men; of this I have a thousand proofs. First of all, I will point you to the cock, who governed the Persians before all other monarchs, before Darius and Megabazus.
1.485: It's in memory of his reign that he is called the Persian bird.
1.486:
**Euelpides**
For this reason also, even to-day, he alone of all the birds wears his tiara straight on his head, like the Great King.
1.488:
**Pisthetaerus**
He was so strong, so great, so feared, that even now, on account of his ancient power,
1.490: everyone jumps out of bed as soon as ever he crows at daybreak. Blacksmiths, potters, tanners, shoemakers, bathmen, corn-dealers, lyre-makers and armorers, all put on their shoes and go to work before it is daylight.
1.492:
**Euelpides**
I can tell you something about that. It was the cock's fault that I lost a splendid tunic of Phrygian wool. I was at a feast in town, given to celebrate the birth of a child; I had drunk pretty freely
1.495: and had just fallen asleep, when a cock, I suppose in a greater hurry than the rest, began to crow. I thought it was dawn and set out for Halimus. I had hardly got beyond the walls, when a footpad struck me in the back with his bludgeon; down I went and wanted to shout, but he had already made off with my mantle.
1.499:
**Pisthetaerus**
Formerly also the kite was ruler and king over the Greeks.
1.500:
**Leader of the Chorus**
The Greeks?
**Pisthetaerus**
And when he was king, he was the one who first taught them to fall on their knees before the kites.
1.501:
**Euelpides**
By Zeus! that's what I did myself one day on seeing a kite; but at the moment I was on my knees, and leaning backwards with mouth agape, I bolted an obolus and was forced to carry my meal-sack home empty.
1.504:
**Pisthetaerus**
The cuckoo was king of Egypt and of the whole of Phoenicia.
1.505: When he called out cuckoo, all the Phoenicians hurried to the fields to reap their wheat and their barley.
1.507:
**Euelpides**
Hence no doubt the proverb, Cuckoo! cuckoo! go to the fields, ye circumcised.
1.508:
**Pisthetaerus**
So powerful were the birds that the kings of Grecian cities, Agamemnon, Menelaus, for instance,
1.510: carried a bird on the tip of their scepters, who had his share of all presents.
1.511:
**Euelpides**
That I didn't know and was much astonished when I saw Priam come upon the stage in the tragedies with a bird, which kept watching Lysicrates to see if he got any present.
1.514:
**Pisthetaerus**
But the strongest proof of all is that Zeus, who now reigns,
1.515: is represented as standing with an eagle on his head as a symbol of his royalty; his daughter has an owl, and Phoebus, as his servant, has a hawk.
1.517:
**Euelpides**
By Demeter, the point is well taken. But what are all these birds doing in heaven?
1.518:
**Pisthetaerus**
When anyone sacrifices and, according to the rite, offers the entrails to the gods, these birds take their share before Zeus.
1.520: Formerly men always swore by the birds and never by the gods. And even now Lampon swears by the goose whenever he wishes to deceive someone. Thus it is clear that you were once great and sacred,
1.523:
**Pisthetaerus**
but now you are looked upon as slaves, as fools, as Maneses; stones
1.525: are thrown at you as at raving madmen, even in holy places. A crowd of bird-catchers sets snares, traps, limed twigs and nets of all sorts for you; you are caught, you are sold in heaps
